1:
Why the chapter stands where it does is answered by two voices. Keil and Delitzsch make the ruin of Saul the introduction to the history of David's kingship, which then runs in two sections, a consecutive narrative of the reign down to the numbering of the people, and a second part on the preparations for the temple and the old king's last commands, of which the first runs parallel to the earlier history and the second is peculiar to this book. Henry says the same thing from the writer's intention: the design is to preserve the records of the house of David, so the reign of Saul is not repeated but only his death, by which a way was made for David to the throne. Clarke, finding the history almost word for word the same as the older account, declines to comment and refers the reader back to his notes there.

Henry supplies the chapter's moral reading in three steps. Princes sin and the people suffer: Israel was not at this time guilty of the idolatry of the judges' days, Samuel having reformed them, and yet they are given to the spoil, because what divine justice chiefly had in view was the sin of Saul, so that great men should take heed of provoking God's wrath, since if they kindle that fire they do not know how many may be consumed for their sakes. Parents sin and the children suffer: his sons perished with him, Jonathan among them, that gracious and generous man, for all things come alike to all. And sinners suffer at last themselves, though long reprieved. On that third head Henry sets the manner of the fall against the sins point by point. Saul had thrown a javelin at David and missed, and the archers hit him. He had commanded Doeg to kill the priests, and now commands his own armour-bearer to run him through. He had disobeyed God in not destroying the Amalekites, and his armour-bearer disobeys him in not destroying him. The murderer of the priests is left to be his own murderer, and the family that cut off the city of the priests is itself cut off.

For the ground and the course of the battle Ellicott carries almost the whole weight. The opening is abrupt, as elsewhere in the prophets; the field was the plain of Jezreel, scene of so many of the struggles of ancient history; and the mountain the beaten army fell back on rises out of that plain to a height of one thousand seven hundred feet. He notes that the word for the men of Israel is singular and collective, which gives a more vivid image of a rout, men fleeing as one body where the older account has the plural. The pursuit he renders as the Philistines cleaving to Saul, since the death of the king and his sons would make the triumph complete; and he observes that the fourth son was not in the battle, that Jonathan at least would not have been far from him at the end.

At the centre of the account stands a phrase the voices do not read alike. Henry's correspondence depends on the archers having hit Saul. Ellicott renders the clause otherwise: they that shoot with the bow came upon him, and he shuddered before the shooters, the verb being properly to writhe or travail, and he treats the terror as natural in a man who believed himself forsaken of God and stood after a lost battle beset by foes he could not reach, with no chance of a fair encounter hand to hand. The request that followed turned on the word for abuse, which means strictly to make a toy of; Saul preferred death by a friendly stroke to the thrusts of insulting enemies. The armour-bearer's refusal Ellicott puts down to loyalty and perhaps dread of the foe.
8:
The stripping of the body and the sending round of the head and armour draw the same judgement from two directions. Ellicott notes the strictly local conception of deities implied in the act, as if their idols could neither see nor hear beyond their own temples, and reads the verb for carrying tidings as one used of good news especially. Henry turns that into an argument against the victors and against ourselves: poor idols, that knew not what was done a few miles off till the tidings were brought to them, nor then either; and if we give not God the glory of our successes, even the Philistines will rise up in judgment against us and condemn us, for shall Dagon have so honourable a share in their triumphs and the living God be forgotten in ours? Wesley carries the same question over in a few words of his own. Henry's other lesson from the spectacle is that the greater dignity men are advanced to, the greater the disgrace they are in danger of falling into, since Saul's body was abused more than any other of the slain because he was king, and advancement makes men a mark for malice.

Where the older account is not word for word the same, Ellicott's reading of the differences is that they point to a second source rather than to corruption. The house of their gods stands here for the house of Ashtaroth, which he thinks the chronicler paraphrased from a repugnance to naming the idol, and he fills out who she was: a great temple at Ascalon as Heavenly Aphrodite, the Queen of Heaven worshipped by the Semitic races generally, Ishtar among the Assyrians with famous temples at Nineveh and Arbela, Athtâr among the Sabæans, and the name Ashtâr coupled with Chemosh on the Moabite Stone. For Dagon he cites the cuneiform inscriptions and the name Ismi-Dagan. The sharper divergence is that the skull, gulgôleth, is fastened in the house of Dagon here, where the older book has the corpse fastened to the wall of Beth-shan. Ellicott calls it hardly likely that either reading is a corruption of the other, and supposes the chronicler found the fact about the head in his additional source, unless the clause has dropped out of the other text.

The burial at Jabesh is read for its motive by one voice and for its rites by another. Clarke sends the reader back to the older account for the principles of heroism and gratitude from which the action proceeded, promising a further illustration from a literary friend at the chapter's end. Ellicott works through the wording: every man of valour; gûfâh for the body, an Aramaic word read nowhere else in the Old Testament; and the burning that the older account mentions and this one does not. Burning a corpse was a further degradation of executed criminals, so he takes the phrase either as making a burning for them of costly spices, as was done at the funerals of kings, or else as a real cremation in this exceptional case because the bodies had been mutilated, noting that the bones buried here, set against the corpses carried off, do seem to imply it. The tree is a terebinth where the other text has a tamarisk, another mark of the second source, and the seven days' fast he compares with the friends of Job and with Ezekiel among the exiles at Tel-abib. Henry draws from the rescue only that a respect is due to the remains of the deceased, and that we are not to enquire concerning the eternal state, which must be left to God.
13:
The closing verdict names two counts, and the voices agree on what they are before they divide over what is missing. Ellicott sets out the unfaithfulness as twofold: Saul did not observe the prophetic word of Jehovah, and he consulted a necromancer to the neglect of consulting Jehovah, so that he broke the general law of his people as well as special commands addressed to himself. He then observes what the verdict passes over, that no allusion is made to the cruel slaughter of the priests nor to the implacable hatred of David. On that silence the other voices are instructive. Clarke gives the Targum in full, which supplies exactly the missing count: Saul did not ask counsel from before the Lord by Urim and Thummim, for he had slain the priests that were in Nob. Gill reports the same addition and refuses it in a clause, that it is not in the text. The one commentator notices an omission, a second finds an ancient reading that repairs it, and the third declines the repair as an addition rather than an exposition.

The flat statement that Saul enquired not of the Lord has to be squared with the older narrative, where he did enquire and received no answer, and three voices square it the same way, by making the enquiry no true enquiry. Ellicott holds that we shall not be reading a meaning of our own into the text if we say that Saul's natural impatience betrayed him again, since he at once despaired of help from his God instead of seeking it with self-humiliation and penitence. Gill allows that he did enquire in some sense, but in an external, careless and hypocritical manner, not seriously nor with constancy, so that it was accounted as if he had not enquired at all. Wesley says the same by degrees, that it was not humbly and penitently, not diligently and importunately, and not until he was brought to the last extremity, and then it was too late. Ellicott draws the whole book's lesson out of the single word: the sin that ruined the first king was essentially that which led to the final ruin of the nation, unfaithfulness to the covenant-God. On the clause that God slew him, he answers that God acts through the instrumentality of His creatures, here the Philistines and the suicidal hand of Saul himself, as later the Assyrian conquerors were made the scourge of guilty peoples and Cyrus was raised up to fulfil all His pleasure. The kingdom turned to David by means of the warriors of Israel.

Clarke closes with a long letter from a literary friend on why the men of Jabesh risked themselves for the bodies. The strong impulse of gratitude prompted them: they remembered their own preservation from destruction and, what to brave men is more galling, from bearing the marks of having been defeated, so that the verses should be read in conjunction with the attack of Nahash. The correspondent then sets the episode beside the father of Grecian poetry, who relates how severe were the contests for the body of a fallen chief, more determined oftentimes than the struggle for victory, a point of military honour perhaps heightened by the prevalent idea about the fate of the spirits of those left unburied. He compares the conduct of the Philistines toward Saul with that of the hero of the Iliad toward Hector, each of the dead men having long been the scourge or the shield of the other's nation. Two further observations are his own: that the Philistines could only have reached Mount Gilboa by a march through great part of the kingdom of Israel, which Saul's absorbing pursuit of David may account for, and that such private matters as the friendship of Jonathan and David are not the things likely to occur to a forger of a narrative.
